headline: Utah: 7 of 12 medical cannabis producers missed DEA's window
dek: Utah's attorney general has joined two other states in backing a court challenge to DEA's 29 November limit, which would have split Utah's supply chain.
key_points: Seven of Utah's 12 medical cannabis cultivators and processors and two of its 14 pharmacies did not apply to DEA in time, according to a state court filing cited by The Salt Lake Tribune.
Under DEA's 29 November limit, Utah's registered pharmacies could have bought only from the five producers that applied, a 58% cut in the producers they could use.
Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, with the attorneys general of North Dakota and West Virginia, filed a brief on 24 November backing Utah company Standard Wellness's request for an injunction.
The D.C. Circuit paused the limit late on 25 November, but said its order is not a ruling on the merits; Utah had 118,238 active patient cards in October.
body: Utah has become the clearest example of what DEA's new medical cannabis trading rule would do to a small, tightly regulated state market. According to a state court filing cited by The Salt Lake Tribune on 26 November, seven of Utah's 12 licensed cultivators and product makers, and two of its 14 medical cannabis pharmacies, did not apply to DEA in time to be treated as applicants under the agency's rescheduling process.

That matters because DEA said in October that businesses which missed the first application round could not trade with those that applied. Had the limit taken full effect on Sunday, 29 November, Utah's market would have been cut in two. Late on 25 November, a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., paused the limit, as we reported this morning. Utah's attorney general is now among the officials asking the court to block it for good.
## A market split in two

The Tribune's account, drawn from the state filing, shows how lopsided the split would have been. The seven producers that missed the deadline would have been left able to supply only the two pharmacies that also missed it. The registered pharmacies, in turn, could have bought only from the five producers that did apply.

On our arithmetic, that means Utah's registered pharmacies would have lost access to 58% of the state's licensed producers overnight. The producers that missed the window would have kept access to just two of 14 storefronts. In a market where every product must be grown and made inside the state, there is no outside supply to fill that gap.

The scale of the patient base explains the alarm. Utah counted 118,238 active medical cannabis cards in October, according to state data cited by the Tribune; the state's Center for Medical Cannabis publishes the monthly figures on its program data page. Businesses and officials quoted by the paper warned that the rule could cause shortages for those patients.
> Utah shows the DEA cut-off is not a paperwork problem. In a closed state market, it decides which pharmacies can stock which shelves.
## How the businesses got caught

The Tribune lays out the sequence. After President Trump's executive order, DEA said in April that it would move medical marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III. DEA then set a June deadline for medical pharmacies to apply for federal registration, allowing them to keep operating under state rules while their applications are reviewed. Producers had a separate window.

Many producers, the paper reports, did not learn of their deadline or of the separate route for applying in time, and DEA later reopened its portal. Then, in October, the agency said that pharmacies and producers that had not applied in the first round could not do business with those that had.

Two Utah companies show how that played out. Dragonfly Wellness, based in Salt Lake City, told the Tribune it would have been unable to sell its own plants and products in its pharmacies in Salt Lake City and Price. Narith Panh, its chief growth officer, said the company would not stop serving patients. Beehive Farmacy applied for its retail permit but not its production permit in time, according to chief executive Bijan Sakaki; the company is moving its pharmacy from Salt Lake City to Draper. Sakaki told the paper that DEA had been unable to give local representatives a clear answer on timing.
## Utah's attorney general joins the fight

On 24 November, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, joined by the attorneys general of North Dakota and West Virginia, filed a brief supporting an injunction request by Standard Wellness, a Utah company that has sued DEA in federal court in Washington, D.C. According to the Tribune, Brown's brief argues that DEA's approach "runs roughshod over Utah's deliberate regulatory scheme."

State officials are not hopeful that DEA will change course on its own. Brandon Forsyth, who runs Utah's medical cannabis division, told the paper the agency has given no sign it will modify its approach. Evan Vickers, the incoming Utah Senate president and a pharmacist, said DEA's action pushes the state's pharmacies into unfamiliar territory.

The Justice Department's position, as summarised by the Tribune, is that Congress gave the federal government power to regulate marijuana, that the businesses are at fault for not applying in time, and that blocking the rule would interfere with enforcement. We covered the department's filing on 24 November.
## What the pause does and does not do

The D.C. Circuit's 25 November order holds back the trading limit while the court considers requests from the industry, and now several states, to block it permanently. The court stressed that its stay should not be read as a ruling on the merits. For now, Utah's producers and pharmacies can keep trading as they did before, but the companies that missed DEA's window remain outside the federal process.

That leaves Utah businesses planning around two possible outcomes. If the court lifts the pause, the split described in the state filing would return. If the court blocks the limit, the question moves to how and when DEA lets late applicants into the federal system. Neither the court nor DEA has given a date for that answer.
## Why other states are watching

Utah's numbers are unusually stark, but the problem is not unique to Utah. The companies challenging DEA include operators from several states, and North Dakota and West Virginia signing on to Utah's brief suggests state governments see the same risk for their own programs. Medical-only states with in-state production rules have the least room to absorb a sudden supply break, because they cannot import product to cover it.
## What to watch

The first signal is how quickly the D.C. Circuit rules on the injunction requests now that it has paused the 29 November limit. The second is whether DEA reopens or extends its application window for producers and pharmacies that missed the first round, which would shrink the problem without a court ruling. In Utah, watch the October-to-November card counts on the state's program data page and any statement from the Center for Medical Cannabis on supply if the pause is lifted.
